title: Genomics and Biotechnology
seo_title: Anatomy and Physiology 12: Genomics and Biotechnology Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
short_title: PCR, gel electrophoresis, recombinant DNA and ethics
standard_text: Genomics and biotechnology: recombinant DNA, PCR, gel electrophoresis and DNA profiling, gene therapy, and the uses and ethics of biotechnology. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Anatomy and Physiology 12)
meta_desc: Free Anatomy and Physiology 12 worksheets (BC Curriculum): PCR, gel electrophoresis, recombinant DNA and ethics. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: PCR copies DNA; gel electrophoresis sorts it by size.
key_sub: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences.
body_html:
How to think about it

Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences, and ligase joins pieces to make recombinant DNA, for example putting the human insulin gene into bacteria. PCR (polymerase chain reaction) makes millions of copies of a DNA segment.

Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size: small pieces move farther. DNA profiles are used in forensics and paternity testing. Biotechnology raises ethical questions about privacy, safety and genetically modified organisms.

Example

In gel electrophoresis, which fragments travel farthest?

Small things move easily.

Answer: the smallest

Example

What does PCR do?

Chain reaction

Answer: makes many copies of DNA

Common mistakes

  • Thinking large fragments move farther in a gel.
  • Thinking PCR makes proteins.
  • Mixing up restriction enzymes and ligase.

faq.q: How is human insulin made today?
faq.a: Bacteria with the human insulin gene make it.
Treating a disease by adding or fixing a gene in a person's cells.

items.q: What is an ethical issue with genetic testing?
c: privacy: insurers or employers might use the results
items.e: Genetic counselling helps people decide.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 1500 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 150, 400. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 1500): 1100, 250, 150. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: How is DNA profiling used in forensic science?
c: reading a person's whole genome every time
comparing the lengths of short tandem repeats from crime-scene DNA and suspects
items.e: STR patterns are almost unique to each person.

items.q: What is genetic fingerprinting based on?
c: genes that are the same in everyone
variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs), which differ between people
items.e: The pattern of bands is compared.

items.q: What is a silent mutation?
c: a base change that does not change the amino acid, because the code is degenerate
a mutation that changes many amino acids
a mutation that stops all transcription
items.e: The protein is unchanged.

items.q: What is an ethical concern about genetically modified crops?
c: genes could spread to wild plants, and there may be less biodiversity
items.e: Benefits include higher yields and pest resistance.

items.q: What is needed for PCR?
c: DNA, primers, free nucleotides and Taq DNA polymerase
items.e: A thermal cycler changes the temperature.

items.q: Why are bacteria treated with calcium ions and heat shock in genetic engineering?
c: to make the cell wall and membrane more permeable to plasmids
items.e: This is transformation.

items.q: What are the three temperature steps in each PCR cycle?
items.e: A heat-stable polymerase (Taq) is used.

items.q: How does gel electrophoresis separate DNA fragments?
c: by size: smaller fragments move further towards the positive electrode
items.e: DNA is negatively charged.

items.q: What is CRISPR-Cas9 used for?
c: editing a specific DNA sequence by cutting it with a guide RNA
items.e: It can knock out or change genes.

items.q: Why is Taq polymerase used in PCR?
c: it is not denatured at high temperatures
items.e: It comes from a bacterium in hot springs.

items.q: What is a DNA probe used for?

items.e: Probes are labelled with fluorescent or radioactive markers.

items.q: What is personalised medicine?
c: treatment chosen to suit a person's genome
items.e: Genome sequencing makes it possible.

items.q: Why are mutations important for evolution?
c: they are the original source of new alleles and genetic variation
items.e: Most are neutral; some are harmful, a few helpful.

items.q: Why is PCR heated to about 95 °C?
c: to separate the DNA strands by breaking hydrogen bonds
items.e: Primers anneal at about 55 °C; extension at 72 °C.

items.q: What do restriction enzymes do?
c: cut DNA at specific base sequences
items.e: They often leave sticky ends.

items.q: Each PCR cycle takes 5 minutes. How many cycles can be completed in 75 minutes, and so how many times larger is the DNA amount?
items.e: 15 cycles; amount × 215 = 32768.

items.q: What is genetic screening used for?
c: finding people who carry particular alleles
items.e: Genetic counselling then explains the risks.

items.q: What is a sticky end?

items.e: Complementary sticky ends can join.
